subject: Cooking
title: Cinnamon Wars: Empire Over Bark
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Cinnamon Wars: Empire Over Bark.

hook.text: Three European empires went to war over tree bark. The prize? Control of the cinnamon trade.

buildup.text: True cinnamon grows only in Sri Lanka. Portuguese colonizers seized the island's supply in 1505.

discovery.text: The Dutch ousted Portugal in 1658, then the British took over in 1796 — all for cinnamon monopoly.

twist.text: Most 'cinnamon' sold today is actually cassia — a cheaper, stronger relative from China and Indonesia.

climax.text: True Ceylon cinnamon is delicate and complex. Cassia is what most people have actually tasted.

punchline.text: Empires fought over a spice most people have never tasted.

quiz.question: Where does true Ceylon cinnamon originate?

details.summary: Cinnamon comes from the inner bark of tropical trees and drove centuries of colonial warfare as European powers fought to control its source. Ceylon cinnamon from Sri Lanka is delicate and complex while cassia from China and Vietnam is stronger and cheaper.
details.whyItMatters: The cinnamon trade shaped colonial empires and global commerce for centuries. The ongoing confusion between true cinnamon and cassia affects both flavor and health considerations.
takeaways: Ceylon cinnamon is mild; cassia is stronger and contains more coumarin
Portugal, Holland, and Britain waged wars over cinnamon control
Most affordable cinnamon sold worldwide is actually cassia bark

faq.question: What is the difference between Ceylon cinnamon and cassia?
faq.answer: Ceylon cinnamon has a delicate, complex, citrusy flavor with thin, layered bark rolls. Cassia is bolder and spicier with thick, single-scroll bark. Cassia contains significantly more coumarin, which can stress the liver in large doses. Ceylon is safer for daily use.

faq.question: Why did European empires fight over cinnamon?
faq.answer: Cinnamon was one of the most valuable commodities in medieval trade, worth more than silver. Portugal seized Sri Lanka's cinnamon monopoly in 1505. The Dutch took it by force in 1658. Britain acquired it in 1796. Control of the supply meant enormous wealth and power.
